vignette:
He is 24, a South Asian man working in diplomacy, and when he talks about the beginning of it, he does not start with the day he leaves the war zone. He starts with the weeks before, when the city still has routines and people are still pretending that routines mean safety. He is posted there early in his career, proud of the assignment, flattered that someone his age is trusted with real responsibility. He spends his days drafting cables, translating nuance across languages, arranging meetings that may or may not happen depending on which roads are open and which buildings are still standing. He learns how quickly professional language can become surreal. “Deteriorating conditions” means smoke visible from the embassy windows. “Civilian impact” means the little grocery below his apartment no longer exists.

At first he tells himself that being useful protects him. He keeps his shirt pressed, answers messages immediately, escorts frightened visitors through checkpoints with a calm voice he does not feel. He calls his partner at odd hours and says he is tired, busy, fine. Then the shelling moves closer. One afternoon, as he is riding in a convoy after visiting a cultural office, the blast comes from the side of the road with a force so sudden that his mind cannot place it. There is a sharp white sound, then dust, metal, shouting. He remembers his face against the seat in front of him, the taste of grit in his mouth, and the driver making a sound he has never heard another person make. He crawls out through a bent door and sees a man on the pavement not moving, one of the local staff members he had been joking with minutes earlier. For a few seconds everything is silent in him. Then his body starts shaking so violently he cannot make his hands work.

After that day, the city changes completely. Or maybe, he says, he changes and the city only reveals itself. Every bang becomes a rehearsal for death. He cannot walk past parked cars without scanning underneath them. He memorizes exits, stairwells, blast walls. He sleeps in bursts, fully dressed, phone and passport beside him. When he does sleep, he jerks awake before dawn with his heart racing, sure that he has heard the impact again. He sees the local staff member’s body whenever he closes his eyes for too long. During one rocket attack he lies on the floor of his apartment bathroom, cheek pressed to tile, and thinks with sudden clarity that he is going to die in a room where he keeps spare soap.

He is eventually evacuated, and people around him use the language of relief. He is lucky. He is safe now. His partner meets him at the airport and holds him so tightly that he feels almost angry, because her softness makes no sense to his body. Back home, the quiet is intolerable. A bus braking hard outside makes him duck. Fireworks send him into the hallway before he knows where he is. In restaurants he has to face the door; if he cannot, he keeps tracking reflections in the window. He avoids news from the region and then, guiltily, checks it obsessively at 3 a.m. He has stopped calling some former colleagues because he cannot bear hearing who has been injured, who is missing, who stayed behind.

At work, he is still polished enough to fool people for stretches of time. He can write elegant briefing notes and sit through formal meetings with his face composed. Diplomacy has taught him how to speak in measured tones, and now that skill becomes a kind of disguise. But concentration slips away from him mid-sentence. A slammed folder in a conference room sends a jolt through him so strong that he loses track of the discussion. He rereads the same paragraph of a cable five times. He is ashamed of how much energy it takes to do ordinary tasks. He used to enjoy the complexity of his work; now every urgent email feels like a threat.

His partner tells him he is present and absent at the same time. He wants closeness, but when she reaches for him in his sleep he comes awake defensive, breathing hard, sometimes pushing her hand away before he recognizes her. He hates the look on her face afterward. He has become irritable in ways that do not fit how he sees himself—snapping over dishes left in the sink, over delays, over nothing. Then he withdraws, sitting in the dark living room scrolling through security updates he tells himself he no longer needs.

He speaks often about guilt. He survived because of timing, paperwork, chance. Others did not. He thinks about the local staff member’s family and about the messages he has not answered from people still there. Part of him feels he abandoned them; another part knows he had no choice. He can argue both positions persuasively, as if preparing both sides of a brief, and neither argument brings relief.

Now, months later, he looks controlled from the outside: young, articulate, promising, back at his post, still in a relationship, still moving through rooms where careful words matter. Inside, he is braced against a world that no longer feels governed by ordinary rules. He misses the version of himself who could hear a loud noise and think only, “What was that?” instead of, “It’s happening again.”
